title: India Cancelled Its Biggest Medical Entrance Exam Over a Paper Leak. The Supreme Court Wants to Know Why It Keeps Happening.
excerpt: The NEET-UG 2026 was scrapped after question papers were compromised on the eve of the test. The Supreme Court has demanded systemic reforms, a CBI probe is underway, and 24 lakh students are in limbo — again.
body:
For the second time in two years, India's single-window medical entrance examination has been derailed by a paper leak — and this time, the Supreme Court has made clear it is running out of patience.

The National Testing Agency cancelled NEET-UG 2026 on May 8, one day after the exam was administered to roughly 24 lakh students at centres across the country. Within hours of the test, evidence emerged that the question paper had been circulated on messaging platforms before the examination began. The Union government ordered a Central Bureau of Investigation probe, and the NTA pulled the results.

On May 29, a bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe heard petitions filed by the Federation of All India Medical Association and the United Doctors Front, both of which have demanded a complete restructuring of the NTA. The court did not mince words.

**"UPSC has never had a paper leak. NTA needs to learn,"** Justice Narasimha said during the hearing. He added that accountability cannot remain abstract. "The real problem won't stop till actual accountability arises. Not in terms of so-and-so will be liable — it will be effective when we know which individual shoulders the responsibility."

The court directed the NTA to file an affidavit within three days detailing the status of a monitoring committee constituted in November 2024 after the previous year's scandal. It also asked Dr. K. Radhakrishnan, who headed a high-level expert committee, to report on the implementation status of his panel's recommendations. The Union Ministry of Human Resource Development — not the Ministry of Health — was directed to file a separate affidavit on how to build institutional memory and domain expertise within the agency.

## A Pattern That Won't Break

The 2024 NEET-UG exam had also been marred by allegations of paper leaks, leading to a Supreme Court hearing and widespread student protests. Although the court ultimately allowed the 2024 results to stand, it ordered sweeping reforms: Aadhaar-based biometric authentication, AI-powered CCTV monitoring at test centres, mobile phone jammers, and multi-tier oversight mechanisms.

In its affidavit filed ahead of the May 29 hearing, the NTA told the court that most of those reforms had been implemented or were at advanced stages. It disclosed that a High-Powered Steering Committee reviewed preparations for NEET-UG 2026 on April 17, recommending additional safeguards including disaster planning, power verification, and post-exam forensic CCTV analysis.

None of it was enough. The paper leaked anyway.

The NTA acknowledged that NEET-UG 2026 was the only major examination it still conducted in pen-and-paper mode. Every other large-scale NTA exam already uses a Computer-Based Test format. The high-level expert committee had specifically recommended shifting NEET to CBT, and the NTA told the court the transition would be implemented from the next cycle.

## A Re-Exam, Under Siege Conditions

A re-examination has been scheduled for June 21, and the NTA says it will be conducted under what amounts to security architecture borrowed from elections. Chief Secretaries, Directors General of Police, and District Magistrates will be looped into coordination. The Department of Posts has been enlisted. AI-assisted surveillance will monitor every centre in real time.

The Centre told the court that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is personally supervising the matter.

## What This Means for NRI Families

For the Indian diaspora, the NEET crisis hits close to home. Thousands of NRI and OCI-cardholder students sit for the exam each year, either under the NRI quota or the general category. Many families invest years of preparation and significant money in coaching — often splitting households across countries so children can prepare for the test in India.

The exam's integrity is not an abstract governance question for these families. It determines whether their children will secure one of roughly 1.1 lakh medical seats in India. When the exam is cancelled, the cascading disruption — to timelines, to visa plans, to gap-year calculations — is immediate and personal.

The Supreme Court has listed the matter for further hearing in July. The court's stated goal is ensuring the NTA acquires "the physical and intellectual wherewithal" to conduct examinations "without any blemish." Whether that happens before the next cycle remains an open question.
author: Diaspora Desk
